storySections.chapterTitle: III-B. The Great Flood and the Floating Blossoms (1974–1980)
storySections.heading: III-B. The Great Flood and the Floating Blossoms (1974–1980)
storySections.body:
In May of 1974, during the hottest week of summer, their son, Aniruddha, was born.

With two children running through the corridors, the house seemed to recover the exuberant energy of its colonial prime. Soma was fierce, inquisitive, and voracious for literature, climbing into the high window embrasures of the library to read Bankim Chandra and Rabindranath by the fading afternoon light. Aniruddha was contemplative and mechanically inclined; before he was six, he had disassembled his father’s pocket watch and successfully put it back together using a sharpened needle and a pair of brass tweezers.

On his third birthday, Aniruddha took his place against the teak doorframe: *18.05.1977 — Aniruddha — 2 ft 6 in.*

The two parallel ladders of pencil and knife notches began their climb up the jamb, side by side.

Then came the catastrophic monsoon of late September 1978.

For five days and nights, an unrelenting cloudburst broke over the catchment basin of the Ganga and Damodar rivers. Simultaneously, a spring tide of exceptional height surged up the Hooghly from the Bay of Bengal. The river rose fifteen feet above its datum level, overtopping the masonry embankments at Nimtala, Baghbazar, and Ahiritola Ghats.

Within twelve hours, North Kolkata was submerged beneath four feet of swirling, muddy water.

In the alleyway outside 14 Balaram Ghosh Street, the water rose like an incoming tide. It carried with it uprooted banana trees, floating wooden tea stalls, dead rats, and the pungent, brown silt of the Bengal delta.

By midnight of the second day, water began to seep under the heavy mahogany front door, spilling into the entrance hallway.

Nirmal was thirty-four years old, at the absolute summit of his physical strength.

Leaving the children with his mother on the safe second floor, Nirmal and Kalyani went down into the flooded ground floor. The water inside the hallway was six inches deep, swirling around their ankles, cold and muddy against the black-and-white Italian marble tiles.

"The library," Nirmal gasped, wading toward the account room where two hundred years of family papers, land deeds, and rare books were stored in low cupboards. "If the water reaches the third shelf, everything is ruined."

Working together in the dim light of two kerosene lanterns, husband and wife carried three hundred volumes up the marble staircase to the dry first-floor salon. Nirmal carried the heavy lead-sheathed deed boxes; Kalyani carried the wrapped cloth bundles of handwritten genealogies and Sanskrit manuscripts.

Then they tackled the entrance.

Nirmal waded out into the waist-deep flood in the alleyway, making four trips to the nearby coal depot where fifty empty jute gunny sacks were stored under a tin roof. He hauled the sacks back, and together in the courtyard verandah, they shoveled forty bags of sand and gravel, stacking them in a tight, interlocking defensive dike across the front threshold.

For forty-eight hours, they fought the river.

Whenever the flood water seeped through the cracks in the sandbag dike, they bailed it out using two heavy galvanized iron buckets, dumping the water into the courtyard drain which was still functioning on a gravity backflow valve.

By three o'clock in the morning of the fourth day, the rain finally ceased.

The cloud cover broke, revealing a brilliant, star-filled autumn sky. The flood in the street had crested and begun its slow, sluggish retreat back toward the river drains.

Exhausted beyond speech, their muscles trembling with lactic acid, their hands raw and bleeding from the coarse jute twine of the sandbags, Nirmal and Kalyani sat down side by side on the top step of the courtyard verandah.

Between them sat a small brass hurricane lantern, its yellow flame throwing long, flickering shadows across the wet brick arches.

Nirmal looked out into the courtyard.

The inner quadrangle was flooded under three inches of clear rainwater that had collected over the Chunar flagstones. In the center, the parijat tree stood tall in the moonlight. The torrential storm had stripped hundreds of blossoms from its branches.

The entire surface of the standing water was covered in a dense, floating carpet of white flowers. Thousands of white petals with vivid saffron stems drifted in slow, circular eddies across the dark water, glowing like fallen stars in the lantern light. The fragrance that rose from the water was intoxicating—a bittersweet, heavenly perfume of wet stone, night air, and blooming parijat that filled the entire mansion.

Kalyani leaned her wet head against Nirmal’s shoulder. She closed her eyes.

"Nirmal," she whispered softly.

"Yes, Kalyani?"

"Do you smell that?"

"Yes," he said, wrapping his arm around her trembling shoulders. "It is the tree."

"No," Kalyani murmured, her voice filled with an ancient, peaceful certainty. "It is the house. It fought the water with us. As long as we stay inside it, nothing can drown us."

storySections.chapterTitle: III-C. The Load-Shedding Evenings and the Tanpura on the Roof (1975–1977)
storySections.heading: III-C. The Load-Shedding Evenings and the Tanpura on the Roof (1975–1977)
storySections.body:
During the mid-1970s, Calcutta was plunged into the era of the great electrical shortages—the chronic, debilitating "load-sheddings" that became a defining feature of daily life in Bengal.

For six, eight, sometimes twelve hours a day, the thermal power stations at Bandel and Santaldih tripped under mechanical failures and coal shortages, cutting off power to whole swathes of the metropolis without warning. The streetlights died; the ceiling fans ceased their whirring; the refrigerators in the kitchens went warm. In the sweltering humid heat of June and July, when the temperature inside the high-ceilinged rooms reached ninety-eight degrees and the air was thick enough to chew, the interior of 14 Balaram Ghosh Street became an unbreathable brick furnace.

Yet those nights of darkness, which drove modern apartment dwellers into paroxysms of fury, became the most luminous memories of Nirmal's marriage.

Whenever the power failed at dusk, Nirmal would take down the heavy notched brass key from its nail behind the water cistern.

Followed by Kalyani, seven-year-old Soma, and three-year-old Aniruddha, he climbed the spiral iron staircase to the southern roof terrace. He inserted the notched key into the English lock, turned the tumblers with that familiar heavy *clack*, and opened the gate to the night sky.

Up on the roof, the world was completely transformed.

Without the harsh glare of streetlamps and neon signs, Calcutta lay bathed in the pale, ethereal silver of starlight and moonshine. The southern breeze, sweeping across thirty miles of open paddy fields from the delta, blew over the parapet with unbroken freshness, carrying the cool scent of the Hooghly and the salty tang of the distant sea.

Kalyani would spread two large woven reed mats (*madur*) across the cool terracotta tiles of the terrace.

She brought up an earthen pitcher of well water scented with vetiver roots (*khus*), a plate of crisp water chestnuts (*paniphal*), and her Miraj tanpura—a magnificent instrument carved from a single seasoned pumpkin gourd, its neck inlaid with ivory floral motifs that had belonged to her musician grandfather in Chinsurah.

Sitting cross-legged on the mat in her soft cotton sari, her long dark hair loosened to the river breeze, Kalyani would place the gourd of the tanpura upon her right thigh.

*Dha... pa... pa... sa...*

The four bronze and steel strings vibrated with a rich, hypnotic drone that resonated against the terrace parapet.

Kalyani closed her eyes. Her clear, velvety voice rose into the warm night, singing the classical monsoon ragas: *Megh Malhar*, *Desh*, and *Miyan ki Malhar*. Her notes were not loud, but they possessed a pure, unhurried sweetness that floated over the rooftops of Shyambazar, mingling with the rustle of the parijat leaves below and the distant chime of the temple bells at Baghbazar Ghat.

Little Aniruddha would lay his head in his mother's lap, his eyes heavy with sleep, mesmerized by the rhythmic movement of her fingers across the strings. Soma lay on her stomach beside her father, pointing out the constellations—the Great Bear (*Saptarshi*), Cassiopeia, and the pole star—as Nirmal traced the celestial navigation paths he used on the river survey launches.

"Look at the city, Baba," Soma would whisper, gazing out toward the river where the black silhouettes of steam tugs drifted past like ghost ships. "It looks as if there are no people down there. Only trees and water."

"The city is resting, Soma," Nirmal would say, gently stroking his daughter's brow. "When the machines stop, the earth remembers what it was before men built chimneys."

Often, neighbors on adjoining rooftops would emerge onto their terraces, drawn by the sound of Kalyani's music in the darkness. Men in dhotis would lean against their brick parapets, smoking bidis, listening in rapt silence as her voice carried the ancient Sanskrit poetry of Kalidasa's *Meghaduta* into the starlit sky.

When the power was restored at one or two in the morning, accompanied by a distant cheer from the alleys below, no one on the terrace moved.

The electric fans in the bedrooms could spin as fast as they pleased, but the children were fast asleep on the reed mats, cradled by the south wind, and Nirmal and Kalyani sat side by side in the dark, watching the constellations wheel overhead until the first pale grey light of dawn broke over the river.

storySections.heading: The Four Continuity Relics of 14 Balaram Ghosh Street
storySections.body: Across eighty years, the physical continuity of the Roy household was anchored by four unchanging physical artifacts: the notched brass key to the southern terrace gate, the parijat tree planted in 1950, the 1928 Junghans pendulum wall clock wound every Sunday at eight, and the Burma teak doorframe of the ground-floor library recording sixty-seven years of family heights.

storySections.chapterTitle: IV. The Promoter's Briefcase and the Unchanging Stones (1981–1992)
storySections.heading: IV. The Promoter's Briefcase and the Unchanging Stones (1981–1992)
storySections.body:
Time in an old North Kolkata mansion does not flow like a river; it settles like river silt, layer upon fine layer, hardening into permanence.

By 1986, Nirmal had risen to Chief Hydrographic Surveyor of the Calcutta Port Trust. His hair at forty-two had silvered at the temples, giving him an air of austere maritime authority. Every morning at eight o'clock, wearing a stiffly starched white bush-shirt with brass surveyor’s buttons and crisp trousers pressed by the neighborhood dhobi, he walked down the marble staircase, kissed Kalyani’s forehead by the pantry door, and boarded the green-and-cream tram at the Shyambazar terminus for the thirty-minute journey to Port Trust House on Strand Road.

The city around them was undergoing an aggressive, chaotic metamorphosis.

The old British street names were being replaced with names of regional political leaders; the open gardens of Central Avenue were being choked with automobile exhaust; the first underground Metro railway was tearing through the red clay beneath Chittaranjan Avenue. Everywhere in Shyambazar and Baghbazar, the grand nineteenth-century brick mansions—the houses of timber merchants, salt traders, and colonial barristers—were being bought up by speculative building promoters. Demolition squads with sledgehammers smashed down century-old cornices, cast-iron verandahs were sold for scrap iron by the hundredweight, and hideous five-story concrete boxes clad in glazed ceramic tiles sprang up like mushrooms in the narrow lanes.

In the winter of 1991, the promoters came for 14 Balaram Ghosh Street.

On a chilly Tuesday afternoon, an expensive white Maruti 1000 car stopped at the mouth of the alleyway. A man named Tapan Roychowdhury, wearing a safari suit of brown polyester and a heavy gold signet ring on his pinky finger, climbed the marble staircase to the first-floor salon. He was accompanied by an architect carrying a black leather portfolio.

Nirmal received them in the salon. He had Haripada serve them tea in fine bone china cups with butter biscuits.

Roychowdhury unrolled a large architectural elevation across the mahogany center table, weighing down the corners with two brass paperweights.

"Mr. Roy," Roychowdhury began, leaning forward with an oily, practiced smile. "Let us speak plainly. This plot is seven cottahs and twelve chittaks. It is a prime corner location. But look at what you have here: three stories of crumbling brick, damp rising through the surki mortar, ancient wiring, sixteen-foot ceilings that cost a fortune to paint, and a roof that probably leaks every July."

Nirmal took a sip of tea. He said nothing.

"My proposal is very generous," Roychowdhury continued, tapping the blueprint with his gold ring. "We demolish this obsolete structure. In eighteen months, we erect a modern residential complex: *Shyam Kunj*. Sixteen three-bedroom apartments with Italian marble flooring, high-speed elevator, standby generator, and covered parking. As the owner of the land, you will receive forty percent of the built-up area—that is six full flats—plus seventy-five lakhs of rupees in liquid cash upon signing the joint venture agreement. You can keep one flat for yourself, give one to each of your children, and rent out the other three. You will be a wealthy man, Mr. Roy. Why live in a museum when you can live in luxury?"

Nirmal sat quietly in his cane armchair.

He did not look at the blueprints of *Shyam Kunj*. He looked past the promoter’s shoulder, out through the arched opening of the verandah into the quadrangle below.

The parijat tree, now forty-one years old, was in green leaf, its thick, moss-covered trunk anchored deep into the soil. In the shade of the branches, Kalyani was sitting on a low wooden piri, cutting fresh green spinach with her mother-in-law's boti, humming an old song from Tagore’s *Gitanjali*.

On the wall behind the promoter, the 1928 Junghans clock measured the seconds with its heavy, wooden heartbeat: *tock... tick... tock... tick.*

Nirmal set his teacup down on the saucer with a soft, dry click.

"Mr. Roychowdhury," Nirmal said. His voice was very quiet, but it had the unmistakable ring of a naval officer commanding an engine room. "When my grandfather built this house in 1892, he used bricks that were soaked in water for three weeks to test their density. The beams overhead are first-grade teak from Moulmein, felled before the railway came to Burma. This house has survived the cyclones of 1942, the Japanese air raids, the communal riots of 1946, and the great flood of 1978. It has sheltered my grandfather, my father, my mother, my wife, and my children."

He stood up from his chair.

"A house is not a commodity, Mr. Roychowdhury. It is not an asset to be liquidated for pieces of printed paper. It is a member of our family. You do not sell your grandfather to a butcher because his knees are stiff. Please take your drawings and your gold ring and leave my house. Haripada will see you to the gate."

Roychowdhury stared at him in disbelief, his face flushing dark red.

"You are an eccentric old fool, Mr. Roy!" Roychowdhury snarled as he rolled up his tracing paper. "In twenty years, you will be dead, your children will be living elsewhere, and this house will collapse into a heap of red dust!"

"If it collapses," Nirmal replied calmly, standing straight beside the door, "it will collapse with its honor intact. Good day, sir."

storySections.chapterTitle: IV-B. The Wedding of Soma and the Key to America (1993–1999)
storySections.heading: IV-B. The Wedding of Soma and the Key to America (1993–1999)
storySections.body:
Yet what money could not tear down, the natural, inevitable passage of generational time began to disassemble.

In the winter of 1993, Soma turned twenty-three. She had completed her Master’s degree in Economics at the Delhi School of Economics with first-class honors, and had fallen in love with a brilliant young research statistician named Parthasarathi, who worked for a scientific institute in Bangalore.

On the night before her wedding, the house at 14 Balaram Ghosh Street was illuminated with hundreds of clay diyas and tiny fairy lights strung along the verandah balustrades.

At midnight, after the relatives had gone to sleep, Soma slipped down to the library.

She found her father sitting at his desk, checking a tidal prediction chart for the Hooghly.

"Baba," she whispered.

Nirmal looked up. He took her hand and walked her to the teak doorframe.

Under the incandescent bulb, the left jamb was covered in a dense, vertical column of pencil notches, knife cuts, and purple ink inscriptions stretching back to 1954.

Nirmal stood her against the wood. He took the bone-handled pocketknife and made the final mark, exactly level with the crown of her head. Beside it, with a steady hand, he wrote:

*12.12.1993 — Soma — 23 yrs — 5 ft 4½ in.*

Soma reached out. Her fingers, decorated with intricate red henna patterns that reached to her elbows, traced the line of her growth: the toddler marks from 1971, the schoolgirl leaps from the 1980s, and now this final, adult boundary.

Tears welled in her eyes and fell onto the timber.

"Baba," she sobbed softly, resting her forehead against his chest. "I am going so far away. Bangalore is a thousand miles from here. What if I forget the sound of the house? What if you paint this door?"

Nirmal stroked her dark hair, his own eyes burning with restrained sorrow.

"Soma," he said gently. "A tree does not forget the rain that watered its roots. You can go to Bangalore, you can go to the moon, but every notch on this teak belongs to you. No one will ever paint over this wood. It is your title deed to this earth."

Four years later, in October of 1997, it was Aniruddha’s turn.

Aniruddha had graduated with the gold medal in Mechanical Engineering from Jadavpur University and had won a prestigious fellowship to pursue his doctorate in computer-aided manufacturing at Ohio State University in Columbus, Ohio.

On the night before his flight to the United States, father and son climbed the spiral cast-iron staircase to the southern roof.

It was a crisp autumn evening. The parijat tree in the courtyard below was in full bloom, sending waves of fragrant, bittersweet perfume up into the cool night air. The vast city of Kolkata lay spread out beneath them—a shimmering carpet of gold and white lights reaching to the distant illumination of the Vidyasagar Setu suspension bridge spanning the river.

Aniruddha stood at the parapet, holding the cold wrought-iron railing.

"Baba," Aniruddha said, his voice tight with anxiety. "I feel guilty leaving you and Ma alone here. The house is eight rooms. The roofs need waterproofing every three years. The plumbing is old. Who will help you when the storms come?"

Nirmal reached into his pocket. He took out the heavy brass terrace key—the four-inch key with the trefoil bow that he had notched with a file on the night of the 1956 heatwave.

The brass was warm and smooth, polished by forty-one years of human handling.

"Take this, Aniruddha," Nirmal said, holding out the key.

Aniruddha looked at his father’s palm in surprise. "Baba, that is the terrace key. How will you get up to the roof?"

"I had a duplicate cut thirty years ago," Nirmal smiled. "This one belongs to you."

He pressed the heavy key into his son's young palm, closing Aniruddha's fingers around the cool metal.

"Listen to me, Aniruddha," Nirmal said, looking out toward the Hooghly where a pilot vessel was steaming down the center channel into the darkness. "When a ship departs from the port of Calcutta and steams out past Sagar Island into the Bay of Bengal, the pilot does not ask the Sagar Island lighthouse to pull up its pilings and sail along behind the ship. The lighthouse stays on the rock. Its only purpose, its only sacred duty, is to keep its lamp burning through every fog and every gale, so that whenever the ship turns back toward home, it knows exactly where the harbor lies."

Nirmal placed his hand over his son's fist.

"Take this key to Ohio. Put it in your desk drawer. Whenever you feel lonely in that foreign country with its frozen winters and strange highways, take this brass in your hand. Remember that 14 Balaram Ghosh Street is standing here, keeping the light on for you."

storySections.chapterTitle: IV-C. The Alpona of Winter and the Saraswati Puja (1987–1990)
storySections.heading: IV-C. The Alpona of Winter and the Saraswati Puja (1987–1990)
storySections.body:
In the winter of 1989, when Soma was nineteen and Aniruddha fifteen, the annual festival of Saraswati Puja transformed 14 Balaram Ghosh Street into a temple of light and art.

For three generations, the Roy family had celebrated the worship of the goddess of learning in the inner quadrangle. Unlike the noisy public street pujas with their blaring cinema loudspeakers and garish plaster idols, the puja at Balaram Ghosh Street was an intimate, monastic festival of intellect, literature, and domestic beauty.

The preparations began three days before the auspicious fifth day of the waxing moon (*Vasant Panchami*).

On the morning before the festival, Kalyani took two pounds of fragrant Gobindobhog rice, soaked it in Ganga water for four hours, and ground it into a silky, milk-white paste (*pituli*) on the heavy black granite grinding stone (*shil-nora*) in the courtyard pantry.

At sunset, Kalyani knelt upon the cold Chunar flagstones of the quadrangle.

She dipped a small wad of washed cotton cloth into the white rice paste, holding it delicately between her thumb and middle finger. Moving backward across the courtyard with practiced, fluid grace, she began to paint the *alpona*—the traditional ritual floor painting that was the ancestral heritage of Bengal's women.

Nirmal stood on the first-floor verandah, looking down at his wife.

Beneath her fingers, the grey stones blossomed into an astonishing, intricate tapestry of white geometric art. She painted creeping vines of parijat flowers with five-pointed leaves, pairs of sacred conch shells (*shankha*), the footprints of the goddess surrounded by circular lotuses, and the elegant, stylized forms of white swans gliding across rippling water.

The lines were astonishingly sharp, flowing from her fingertips with the effortless precision of a master calligrapher.

"Come down, Soma," Kalyani called up softly, her forehead glistening with fine beads of sweat. "It is time you took over the outer border."

Soma, then an undergraduate at Presidency College, knelt beside her mother on the stones. For three hours, mother and daughter worked side by side in the lantern light, their white handloom saris tucked tightly at the waist, their fingers tracing the sacred patterns across fifty square yards of stone.

By midnight, the inner quadrangle was completely covered in a shimmering, lace-like carpet of white rice art that glowed like frost under the winter moon.

At dawn on the day of the puja, the clay idol of Saraswati arrived from the potters' quarter of Kumartuli, carried on a wooden bier by four young craftsmen.

The goddess was seated upon a white swan, holding a polished veena in her hands, her face sculpted with calm, benevolent serenity from the sacred alluvial clay of the Hooghly. She was installed on a raised wooden dais beneath the parijat tree, whose branches were adorned with garlands of yellow marigolds and green mango leaves.

Then came the ritual that defined the intellectual soul of the household: the *Boi-Pujo*—the blessing of the books.

On the steps of the dais, beneath the feet of the goddess, the family stacked the tools of their minds:

Nirmal placed his brass surveyor's octant, his tidal prediction tables, and his grandfather's 1892 Moulmein timber ledger.

Kalyani placed her mother's palm-leaf manuscript of the *Bhagavad Gita* and her silver-inlaid tanpura.

Soma placed her university textbooks on macroeconomics, her volumes of Amartya Sen, and her well-thumbed copies of John Maynard Keynes.

Young Aniruddha placed his sliderule, his German geometry compass set, his calculus notebooks, and a small copper electric motor he had wound with his own hands.

Beside the instruments of learning, two dozen glass inkwells filled with black, blue, and purple ink were placed upon the rice alpona, each holding an unsharpened quill or a bamboo dip pen (*khager kolom*).

When the family priest, an elderly Brahmin from Baghbazar with a voice like a bronze bell, chanted the ancient Vedic mantras, the courtyard echoed with the sacred Sanskrit verses:

*Saraswati namastubhyam, varade kamarupini...*

"O Saraswati, salute to thee, giver of boons, who fulfills all desires. I begin my studies, may there be accomplishment for me always."

Nirmal stood beside his children, his palms joined in prayer.

He looked at the books stacked beneath the clay feet of the goddess—the ledgers of his grandfather, the instruments of his own river career, the economic treatises of his daughter, the mathematical calculations of his son.

Four generations of one family had pursued knowledge not for ostentation or brute accumulation, but as a sacred dialogue with truth.

And around them, the lime-plastered walls and seasoned teak rafters of 14 Balaram Ghosh Street held the chanting, held the fragrance of burning sandalwood and roasted yellow moong dal, holding the family in an embrace that felt as enduring as the river that flowed three blocks to the west.

storySections.quote: When a ship departs from the port of Calcutta, the lighthouse does not pull up its pilings and sail along behind. The lighthouse stays on the rock so the ship always knows where home is.
storySections.attribution: Nirmalendu to his son Aniruddha, October 1997

storySections.chapterTitle: V. The Retirement and the Golden Autumn (2000–2010)
storySections.heading: V. The Retirement and the Golden Autumn (2000–2010)
storySections.body:
In December of 2004, at the age of sixty, Nirmalendu Roy retired from the Calcutta Port Trust after forty-three years of continuous service.

His retirement ceremony was held at the Marine Club on Strand Road. In the presence of eighty river pilots, hydrographers, and port engineers, the Chairman presented Nirmal with a silver-plated scale model of the survey vessel *Pathfinder* and a leather-bound citation commending his exceptional forty-three-year contribution to the safety of navigation on the Hooghly River.

At four o'clock that afternoon, Nirmal boarded the tram for the last time as an active government servant.

He carried the silver ship in a cardboard box under his arm. He stepped down at Shyambazar, walked down the familiar cobblestones of Balaram Ghosh Street, and pushed open the heavy mahogany front door.

The house was breathtakingly quiet.

In 1944, twenty-two voices had echoed across the courtyard. In 1978, children had shouted and raced down the corridors. Now, there was only the steady, wooden ticking of the Junghans clock on the first-floor landing, and the faint, comforting clatter of a brass spoon against an iron saucepan in the kitchen.

Kalyani came out to the hallway, wiping her hands on her apron.

She looked at the cardboard box in his hands, then looked into his eyes. A gentle, knowing smile touched her lips.

"The sailor has come home," she said softly.

"Yes," Nirmal smiled, setting the silver ship down on the marble console table. "The voyage is finished."

The decade that followed was the quiet, golden autumn of their lives.

They settled into an unhurried, monastic routine of two people who had loved each other so deeply and for so long that words had become largely superfluous.

Every morning at five-thirty, Nirmal walked down to Baghbazar Ghat. He took his swim in the cool, flowing water of the Hooghly, watching the morning mists rise from the river as the country boats brought fresh vegetables from the rural districts of Nadia and Hooghly. He returned home carrying a bunch of fresh coriander, sweet winter radishes, and two live pond-carp wrapped in fresh banana leaves.

Kalyani brewed tea in two white porcelain cups—strong CTC tea brewed with crushed ginger, whole green cardamom, and fresh cow's milk.

They drank their tea together on the courtyard verandah, sitting side by side on two cane chairs, watching the white parijat blossoms drift down from the canopy onto the Chunar flagstones.

In the afternoons, Nirmal took over the physical maintenance of the house with the same methodical precision he had once applied to hydrographic charts. He scraped the lime efflorescence from the brick foundations; he oiled the bronze hinges of the sixty-four louvered shutters with linseed oil; he weeded the terrace parapets; every Sunday morning at eight o'clock, with absolute religious fidelity, he stood on his footstool and wound the Junghans clock.

The children visited every winter.

Soma brought her husband and two teenage daughters from Bangalore. Aniruddha, now a senior research director at a robotics firm in America, flew in from Ohio with his wife and their five-year-old daughter, Rimli.

For three weeks every December, the old mansion shook off its silence and erupted into joyous chaos.

Rimli, speaking English with an American Midwestern cadence, was enchanted by the high ceilings, the echo of the stairwell, and the ancient bronze handles.

On a sunlit morning in December 2005, Nirmal took his granddaughter by the hand and led her to the library doorframe.

"Look here, Rimli," he smiled, pointing to the dense thicket of marks. "Here is your father when he was five. And here is your Aunt Soma. Now it is your turn."

He placed the little girl's heels against the teak. With the bone-handled knife, he cut a tiny, perfect groove:

*22.12.2005 — Rimli — 5 yrs — 3 ft 5 in.*

Rimli reached up and touched the groove with her small, smooth thumb.

"Grandpa," she asked, looking up with wide eyes. "Will this mark stay here forever?"

"As long as the house stands, little bird," Nirmal whispered. "It will never leave."

storySections.caption: The courtyard bench beneath the parijat tree where Nirmal and Kalyani shared fifty-four autumns.

storySections.chapterTitle: V-B. The Nor'wester of 2012 and the Final Clock-Winding (2011–2016)
storySections.heading: V-B. The Nor'wester of 2012 and the Final Clock-Winding (2011–2016)
storySections.body:
Then came the bitter, devastating spring of 2011.

It began innocently, with a mild, persistent ache beneath Kalyani's right ribs and an unexplained fatigue that she tried to dismiss as ordinary indigestion from summer heat. By July, however, her appetite had vanished, and her skin had taken on a pale, translucent, lemon-yellow hue.

Nirmal took her to the medical college hospital on College Street.

The ultrasound and biopsy confirmed their worst fears: advanced cholangiocarcinoma—inoperable cancer of the bile ducts. The chief oncologist, an old friend from Scottish Church College, took Nirmal into his private office, closed the door, and placed a hand on his shoulder.

"Three to six months, Nirmal," the doctor said quietly. "Keep her comfortable. Do not subject her to painful interventions that offer no cure."

Nirmal walked out of the hospital into the blinding July sun. He did not cry. He felt only an immense, cold clarity settle over his soul.

He refused to place Kalyani in a sterile hospice or hire professional nurses.

At sixty-seven, he transformed himself into her full-time caregiver. He moved their marriage bed down from the second floor to the ground-floor bedroom adjoining the courtyard, so that Kalyani could look out at her beloved parijat tree without having to climb the marble stairs.

He bathed her frail body with warm water scented with rose petals; he prepared light gruels of sago and green papaya with his own hands; he crushed her painkillers with a brass mortar and pestle; during the long, suffocating nights of the Bengal summer, when the electricity failed and the ceiling fan died, he sat beside her bed with a palm-leaf hand fan, fanning her rhythmically for hours until she fell into a fitful sleep.

In April of 2012, during the season of the violent nor'wester thunderstorms (*Kalbaishakhi*), the end arrived.

On the night of the sixteenth of April, a massive tempest broke over Kolkata. The wind roared at sixty miles an hour, driving torrents of rain against the green shutters, bending the thick branches of the parijat tree, rattling the heavy glass panes of the skylights like machine-gun fire. The city grid collapsed, and total darkness enveloped Shyambazar.

In the bedroom, two brass oil lamps cast flickering golden circles on the lime-plastered walls.

Kalyani was slipping away. Her breathing was shallow, rapid, and raspy; her pulse was a faint, thready flutter beneath Nirmal's fingertips.

Around two in the morning, as the roar of the wind subsided into a steady, rhythmic drumbeat of rain upon the courtyard flagstones, Kalyani opened her eyes.

Her gaze, which had been clouded by morphine, suddenly cleared. She looked at the shadows dancing across the ceiling, then turned her face toward Nirmal.

She reached out with her cold, emaciated right hand and touched Nirmal’s wrist.

"Nirmal," she whispered, her voice barely louder than the rustle of rain.

Nirmal leaned down, kissing her pale, dry lips. "I am here, Kalyani. I am right here beside you."

"The clock upstairs..." she breathed, her chest heaving with the effort. "Did you... did you wind it this morning?"

Nirmal felt a sudden, crushing spasm of agony in his heart.

In the terrifying panic of her sudden decline over the preceding forty-eight hours, he had forgotten the Sunday ritual. For the first time in sixty-two years, the Junghans clock had run down. Its pendulum was still; its springs were slack.

"I will wind it, Kalyani," Nirmal wept, his tears falling onto her cold hands. "I will wind it this very second."

A faint, exquisitely peaceful smile curved the corners of Kalyani’s lips.

"Good," she whispered, closing her eyes. "A house must not stop... while we are in it... keep the heartbeat... going..."

Her hand grew slack in his palm. Her breathing softened, caught once, and gently ceased.

Kalyani was sixty-three years old.

When the relatives and neighbors arrived at dawn with the bamboo bier, the white handloom shroud, and the garlands of tuberoses, they found the front door unlocked.

They walked up the marble staircase to the first floor.

There, in the central salon, stood Nirmalendu Roy.

He had bathed in cold well water. He wore a clean white cotton dhoti. His face was pale as sculpted marble, but his hands were steady. He was standing on the wooden footstool before the Junghans clock, holding the winged brass key.

He inserted the key into the right arbor.

*Crrk... crrk... crrk... crrk.*

He wound the left strike barrel. He took the heavy brass pendulum bob between his fingers, pulled it to the side, and released it.

*Tock... tick... tock... tick.*

The deep, solemn wooden chime filled the empty mansion.

Only then did Nirmal step down from the stool, walk down the stairs, and let the mourners carry his wife out to the river.

storySections.chapterTitle: V-C. The Monsoon Maintenance and the Terrace Gargoyles (2013–2016)
storySections.heading: V-C. The Monsoon Maintenance and the Terrace Gargoyles (2013–2016)
storySections.body:
In the years immediately following Kalyani's death, the physical maintenance of the roof became Nirmal's primary summer liturgy.

Every year in late May, before the first monsoon depression formed over the Andaman Sea, Nirmal prepared 14 Balaram Ghosh Street for the deluge. The flat southern terrace roof was seventy feet by forty feet, covered in square terracotta tiles laid in a bed of surki mortar. Drainage was provided by six cast-iron gargoyles shaped like makara sea monsters, projecting eighteen inches beyond the brick cornice to throw the runoff clear of the exterior walls.

At seventy years of age, Nirmal climbed the spiral iron staircase carrying a wooden bucket of coal tar, a stiff coir brush, and a bamboo clearing rod.

He unlocked the terrace gate with his notched brass key.

He knelt on the terracotta tiles under the heavy, purple-grey pre-monsoon sky. With the bamboo rod, he cleared each makara mouth of dead parijat leaves, bird droppings, and accumulated dust. Wherever the mortar between the tiles had hairline cracks from the blistering April sun, he applied hot coal tar, sealing the joints with rhythmic, deliberate strokes.

As he worked, the first cold gusts of the southwest monsoon would arrive from the river.

The sky would darken from slate to deep charcoal. Across the vast North Kolkata skyline, thousands of pigeons would wheel in panic toward their roosts, and the smell of ozone, wet dust, and river water would herald the deluge.

Then the rain would hit—a solid wall of grey water that turned the terrace into a foaming lake two inches deep.

Nirmal would not hurry downstairs.

He stood beside the brick parapet, his cotton dhoti soaked and clinging to his knees, his face turned upward into the cool, violent downpour. He watched the water rush toward the six makaras. The iron mouths roared as they spouted six arching jets of stormwater into the alleyway below, functioning with the effortless hydraulic capacity his grandfather had engineered in 1892.

"The roof holds, Kalyani," Nirmal would say aloud into the wind, his voice swallowed by the thunder rolling over Baghbazar. "The drainage is clear. The brick is dry underneath."

He knew that as long as the roof was sound, the rooms below were immortal.

The ceilings of Moulmein teak, the ledgers in the library, the ivory dial of the Junghans clock, and the column of height marks on the doorframe would remain safe from the rot that had claimed so many other houses in the neighborhood.

He would lock the iron gate with the brass key, descend the spiral stairs in the darkness, and step into the dry, scented sanctuary of the first floor, feeling the profound satisfaction of a captain whose vessel has weathered another squall without taking a cup of water into the hold.

storySections.chapterTitle: VI. The Solitude and the Fourth Generation (2017–2022)
storySections.heading: VI. The Solitude and the Fourth Generation (2017–2022)
storySections.body:
Grief in an old house does not remain a wound; over the years, it transforms into an architecture of companionship.

After Kalyani’s cremation at Nimtala Ghat, Nirmal lived alone at 14 Balaram Ghosh Street for twelve years.

His children pleaded with him to leave.

"Baba, you cannot live in that enormous house by yourself," Soma begged on the telephone from Bangalore every Sunday evening. "You are seventy-three years old. If you slip on the marble stairs at midnight, who will find you? Come live with us. We have a ground-floor suite with an attached garden. You can teach math to your granddaughters."

"Move to Ohio, Baba," Aniruddha urged from America. "I will file for your permanent residency tomorrow. The winters are snowy, but the house has radiant floor heating. You can spend your days in my workshop."

Nirmal listened to both of his children with immense tenderness, but his answer never varied.

"My dear children," he would reply, seated at his father’s teak desk in the library, looking out at the green parijat canopy. "A banyan tree that has stood eighty years in the soil of North Kolkata cannot be uprooted and planted in a suburban lawn. Its roots are wound around the brick footings of this house. If you take me away from Shyambazar, I will wither into a ghost within six months. Here, every brick remembers your mother. When the south wind blows from the river at night, I hear her footsteps on the verandah. I am not alone. The house is keeping me company."

He kept the mansion with fierce, loving discipline.

Every Sunday at eight o’clock, the Junghans clock was wound. Every morning at dawn, Nirmal took a stiff broom made of coconut ribs and swept the courtyard flagstones, gathering the fallen parijat blossoms into a brass bowl and placing them before Kalyani’s framed portrait on the library mantelpiece. When the monsoons brought rising damp, he scraped the saltpeter; when the white ants attempted to cross the library threshold, he repelled them with mixtures of neem oil and turpentine.

In February of 2021, when Nirmal turned seventy-seven, life gave him an unexpected, breathtaking gift.

Aniruddha’s daughter, Rimli—now twenty-one, an architecture graduate from the University of Illinois—won a prestigious travel fellowship to document the heritage domestic architecture of colonial Calcutta. She arrived at Balaram Ghosh Street to stay for three months.

And with her came her six-month-old daughter, Oindrila.

For ninety days, the old mansion was blessed with four living generations of human presence.

The sound of an infant’s babbling echoed through the high lime-plastered arches. Baby clothes fluttered once again from the wrought-iron terrace balustrades. The smell of warm baby powder mingled with the ancient scent of teak and camphor.

One golden afternoon in late February, Rimli found her grandfather standing in the doorway of the library.

The winter sun was streaming through the fanlight, casting an amber glow across the left doorframe with its sixty-seven years of family notches.

Nirmal was holding baby Oindrila in his arms. The child was laughing, her tiny bare feet kicking against his cotton kurta.

"Bring me the pocketknife and the purple ink from the desk, Rimli," Nirmal said, his voice soft with emotion.

Rimli brought the knife and the ink.

Nirmal held the baby upright, resting her tiny pink heels against the marble threshold at the bottom of the jamb.

"Hold her head steady against the timber for just two seconds, little bird," Nirmal whispered to his granddaughter.

With the bone-handled knife, his aged hands remarkably steady, Nirmal carved a tiny, delicate horizontal line into the dark wood, just twenty-four inches above the floor.

With the dip pen, he wrote beneath it in his precise surveyor’s hand:

*24.02.2021 — Oindrila — 6 mos — 2 ft 0½ in.*

Rimli stood beside him, looking at the doorframe.

Her eyes traveled up the column of marks: her grandfather's first notch from 1954; her father's notches from the 1970s; her own mark from 2005; and now her daughter's notch from 2021.

Four generations of one family, carved into four inches of Burma teak, standing victorious against oblivion.

Rimli put her arms around her grandfather's frail shoulders and wept against his chest.

"Dadu," she whispered. "This doorframe is a miracle. It is more sacred than any temple in India."

Nirmal smiled gently, stroking her hair.

"No, my child," he said softly. "The wood is just wood. It is the love we bring to it that makes it remember."

storySections.chapterTitle: VI-B. The Final Chimes on Balaram Ghosh Street (2023–2024)
storySections.heading: VI-B. The Final Chimes on Balaram Ghosh Street (2023–2024)
storySections.body:
The final November arrived in the year 2024.

On the fourteenth of November, Nirmalendu Roy celebrated his eightieth birthday. He received video calls from Bangalore and Ohio; he saw his great-granddaughter Oindrila running across an autumn lawn in America, shouting "Dadu!" into the screen. He smiled, blessed them all, and told them he was well.

In truth, his body had grown very light and fragile, like a dry bamboo leaf waiting for the first winter wind. His steps on the marble stairs were slow, deliberate, and accompanied by the soft tapping of his ebony walking stick. But his mind remained as clear as the autumn sky above the Hooghly.

On Sunday, the seventeenth of November, he climbed the footstool at eight in the morning and wound the Junghans clock for the last time.

The springs took the turn smoothly: *crrk... crrk... crrk... crrk.* The heavy brass pendulum swung with its ancient, unbroken cadence: *tock... tick... tock... tick.*

Three days later, on the morning of the twentieth of November, Nirmal woke at dawn.

He felt no pain, no fever, no shortness of breath. He felt only a profound, velvety exhaustion—the sensation of a long, heavy ship that has crossed a stormy ocean and finally reached the calm, sheltered waters of its home anchorage.

He bathed in warm water, put on a fresh white cotton kurta, and walked out into the inner quadrangle.

It was six o'clock in the morning.

The parijat tree, seventy-four years after his mother had planted it, was in the glory of its annual bloom. During the night, thousands of flowers had fallen. The grey Chunar flagstones were completely buried beneath an immaculate, snowy blanket of white petals and vivid orange stems. The sweet, heavenly perfume filled the entire courtyard, rising toward the pale morning sky like incense.

Nirmal stood beneath the canopy. He bent down, his knees stiff with eighty years of living, and picked up three fallen blossoms.

He held them in the palm of his right hand.

He walked into the ground-floor library. He did not sit at his desk. He sat down in his father's old high-backed teak armchair beside the doorframe—the chair in which Dhirendranath had sat in 1944.

Through the open green louvered shutters, the morning sounds of North Kolkata floated into the quiet room:

The distant, metallic rumble of the first tram grinding over the rails at Shyambazar five-point crossing.

The deep, mournful steam whistle of a Port Trust launch heading down the Hooghly toward the sea.

The cheerful whistling of the boy delivering milk cans on his bicycle.

The calls of green parakeets swooping down from the parijat tree into the courtyard.

Up on the first floor, the 1928 Junghans clock began to strike eight o'clock.

*Dong... dong... dong... dong... dong... dong... dong... dong.*

The eight golden chimes resonated through the heavy timber beams, vibrated through the lime-plastered brick walls, and sank deep into the cool flagstones beneath his feet.

Nirmal closed his eyes.

He did not feel fear. He did not feel regret. He felt only an immense, infinite gratitude for the eighty years he had been allowed to inhabit this earth, this city, this river, and this house.

He saw the blackout curtains falling in 1947; he saw the southern roof in 1956; he saw Kalyani’s red footprints in 1968; he saw the floating white blossoms in the flood of 1978; he saw four generations of children standing against the teak doorframe.

His breathing slowed, softened, and gently ceased.

His right hand remained open on the wooden armrest of the chair, cradling the three parijat flowers in the golden morning light.

When the neighbor's son came at nine with the morning newspaper, he found the old surveyor sitting peacefully in his chair, with a faint, serene smile upon his lips.

Around him, 14 Balaram Ghosh Street stood silent, sheltering, and faithful.

The brick held his warmth; the teak held his measurements; the clock kept his time; and the parijat showered its blossoms upon the stones that had known his name for eighty years.

We do not own a house; we are merely granted custody of its air, its light, and its shadows for the brief span of our breathing. If we inhabit it with reverence, if we oil its latches and celebrate its seasons, the timber and the brick will return the favor. They will keep our secrets, hold our measurements, and echo our footsteps long after we have returned to the dust.
